The critical points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(a)$ does not exist, where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} & -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=0 \\ -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\ne 0$ for any point $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we must have 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1-2{x}^{2}=0 \\ -2xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get

$$
1-2{x}^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

 

Substituting these values into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-(\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})y=0\,⟹\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$

In conclusion, $f$ has two critical points, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$ Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these two points, they are also both stationary points.
